Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Now I'm comparing the PPIC polls from September and October, which both put the yes side at 58%. The Berkeley IGS poll shows 54% yes, with a slightly larger undecided share, and I'm checking whether its sample description matches the others.

Now I'm checking the Berkeley IGS release, which has 54% yes, 37% no, and 8% undecided. I'm also weighing the AIMSA poll at 56% support, and I'm trying to figure out whether SurveyUSA polled this proposition at all, since the figure I'm seeing may belong to a different measure.

Now I'm weighing a counterpoint: tax measures usually fail in California, but this one extends an existing tax rather than creating a new one, so the base rate may not apply. I'm recalling past extensions like Props 52, 55, and 56, which passed comfortably, and the failures like Prop 15 and the 2018 gas tax repeal, to see whether the comparison holds.

I'm weighing whether the Prop 40 backlash could drag Prop 3 down too, since voters who dislike Prop 40 might reject any tax on the wealthy. The PPIC numbers cut against that, though: Prop 3 sits at 58% yes while Prop 40 is only at 46%, so Prop 3 is clearly holding up better. Opposition spending is tiny compared with support, so the main risks I see are late erosion and turnout shifts.

I'm checking the historical record for California propositions with similar poll support, looking at how final polls compared with results, starting with Prop 30 in 2012.

I'm pulling together the historical comparisons now, recalling how final polls for Prop 30 in 2012 and Props 55 and 52 in 2016 lined up with their results. Since I'm not sure of the exact figures for those earlier polls, I'd like to check them before relying on them.

Next I'm looking for a CalMatters piece from 2019 that says support for propositions tends to slip as Election Day nears, to estimate how much erosion to expect. I also want to see whether the September Berkeley IGS poll had Prop 3 at a different level, so I can judge the trend.

Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

I'm weighing a few risks on the No side: voters confusing Prop 3 with Prop 40 and voting no on both, the tendency of uncertain voters to default to no, fatigue from the number of tax measures, and the possibility that the ballot label shifts opinion. The polls were taken with the official ballot title and label in front of respondents, so those numbers should already reflect that wording.

I'm going to look at the 2019 CalMatters piece again for what it says about tax measures and the decline figures, then check the PPIC "Five Fast Takes" post and the Prop 3 numbers in their time-trends PDF.

content.text: The CalMatters analysis of historical polling suggests support often erodes before Election Day, especially for tax and education measures. I'll check the most recent PPIC commentary and the PPIC trend data for Prop 3.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos

These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects
from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted
sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups is larger. Sampling
error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as
question wording, question order, and survey timing.

Updated Oct. 18, 2019 In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform (http://www.capradio.org/articles/2019/07/17/california-bail-industrys-latest-effort-to-stay-in-business-ask-voters-for-constitutional-protection/), rent control (https://calmatters.org/housing/2019/09/big-rent-hikes-illegal-in-california-heres-what-to-know/), school construction (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/school-bond-breaking-up-with-pge-trade-war-stephon-clark-and-rabbis/) funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Sign up for free Δ That’s based on a bit of conventional wisdom, widely held among the types of people who fixate on such things, that support for ballot measures always declines the closer you get to election day. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos
KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in English and Spanish according to the respondents’
preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place from October
16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects
from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted
sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups is larger. Sampling
error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as
question wording, question order, and survey timing.

Updated Oct. 18, 2019 In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform (http://www.capradio.org/articles/2019/07/17/california-bail-industrys-latest-effort-to-stay-in-business-ask-voters-for-constitutional-protection/), rent control (https://calmatters.org/housing/2019/09/big-rent-hikes-illegal-in-california-heres-what-to-know/), school construction (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/school-bond-breaking-up-with-pge-trade-war-stephon-clark-and-rabbis/) funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. Fact check: Do Californians really cool on ballot measures as the election approaches?

By Ben Christopher, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Updated Oct. 18, 2019

In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform, rent control, school construction funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide.

A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things.

  • Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November.
  • There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the electcademocrats.com tracker may lean partisan, so I'd rely on primary sources where I can. The IGS page lists Proposition 3's certified results as still pending. I'm also keeping in mind the CalMatters 2019 finding that public net support for ballot initiatives dropped by about 7 points a month on average.

I'm weighing the CalMatters finding that voter support for measures tends to erode closer to election day, with the steepest drops in midterm years like 2026. Prop 3's polls look flat from September to October, with net support around +17 to +18. I'm estimating that a typical monthly decline would shave maybe 3 points off that by election day, which still leaves a comfortable margin, though polling error could move it.

The math suggests Yes stays ahead even with some erosion, around 85-95% by my rough estimate. Tax measures tend to sour faster, which argues against Prop 3, though it's an extension and those usually poll better.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters article for more detail on how tax measures have held up, then check the PPIC blogs and the full October report for Prop 3's specific numbers and trend.

I'm checking the PPIC likely-voter trends and the October report for Prop 3's exact numbers, and I'm considering whether the midterm electorate's partisan mix shifts the support picture.

I'm checking whether any campaign against Prop 3 is funded enough to matter. The CalTax "No" committee looks small, and the billionaire-backed group that's targeting Props 40 through 42 doesn't appear to be spending on Prop 3.

I'm weighing a few risks on the No side: voters confusing Prop 3 with Prop 40 and voting no on both, the tendency of uncertain voters to default to no, fatigue from the number of tax measures, and the possibility that the ballot label shifts opinion. The polls were taken with the official ballot title and label in front of respondents, so those numbers should already reflect that wording.

I'm going to look at the 2019 CalMatters piece again for what it says about tax measures and the decline figures, then check the PPIC "Five Fast Takes" post and the Prop 3 numbers in their time-trends PDF.

content.text: The CalMatters analysis of historical polling suggests support often erodes before Election Day, especially for tax and education measures. I'll check the most recent PPIC commentary and the PPIC trend data for Prop 3.
