Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Updated Oct. 18, 2019 In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform (http://www.capradio.org/articles/2019/07/17/california-bail-industrys-latest-effort-to-stay-in-business-ask-voters-for-constitutional-protection/), rent control (https://calmatters.org/housing/2019/09/big-rent-hikes-illegal-in-california-heres-what-to-know/), school construction (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/school-bond-breaking-up-with-pge-trade-war-stephon-clark-and-rabbis/) funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Sign up for free Δ That’s based on a bit of conventional wisdom, widely held among the types of people who fixate on such things, that support for ballot measures always declines the closer you get to election day. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. I'm pulling the main figures from the CalMatters 2019 analysis: support drops about 6.6 to 7 points a month on average. The Kousser/NBER finding is that when the opposition more than doubles spending, support falls about twice as fast, while a well-funded backer keeps measures just above winning.

Now I'm checking the timing pattern: the sharpest declines show up in off-year and midterm primary contests, and much smaller ones before presidential general elections. A 2026 midterm general election is off-year, so the steeper drop-off could still apply. Voters also seem to sour faster on education and tax-raising measures than on bond or tax-cut measures, which matters for Prop 3.

Prop 3's net support barely moved from early September to late October, roughly a single point of erosion across seven weeks, well below the average monthly decline. That fits the pattern where a yes side with far more money holds its ground. The non-presidential timing still points toward some risk, so I'm weighing whether the funding edge outweighs it.

I'm estimating Prop 3's final margin: the current polls sit around +16 to +17 net, and I'm allowing a few points of erosion over the last ten days, which lands the expected final net somewhere near +12 to +16. I also want the sampling error, which for a poll of roughly 1,100 to 1,500 likely voters comes to about 2.7 points before adjusting for design effect.

I'm working out a probability for Prop 3 from the poll numbers and their error margins, which lands near 90% for a Yes win. I'm also checking the historical base rate, since tax measures have passed only about a third of the time, but extensions of existing taxes have done better than new ones.

I'm weighing whether the Prop 3 case parallels earlier measures that passed with little funded opposition, like Prop 55 in 2016 and Prop 30 in 2012, which would suggest a passing margin around 60% or better. I'm also noting that the broader 2026 environment leans Democratic, which should favor a measure that Democrats back strongly, though some erosion from tax fatigue remains a possible risk.

I'm weighing the risks left for Prop 3: tax fatigue from the crowded ballot, and whether late opposition spending or a shift in how the measure is framed could peel off support. Late-counted ballots in California have leaned younger and more Democratic, which should help the yes side rather than hurt it. I'm also checking whether any other pollster has Prop 3 close, but the poll I'm looking at is for a different measure.

I'm checking whether SurveyUSA or any other pollster has released a Prop 3 poll beyond the PPIC, IGS, and AIMSA numbers I've already found. I'm also looking for the Prop 3 trend figures in the PPIC time-trends report to confirm the September-to-October movement.

I'm going to check the PPIC time-trends PDF further in for the Prop 3 question, since it may sit well past the early sections I already read. I also want to scan the rest of the electcademocrats poll listings for any Prop 3 entries I haven't seen yet, beyond the IGS and PPIC numbers I already have.

I'm going to pull up the AIMSA poll article to check who ran it, the "no" share, and the sample size, since I want to know whether the 56% figure comes from a neutral pollster.

I'm settling on the answer format: the user wants only "yes" or "no", so I'll give "yes" for the Yes side being more likely to win, and I'm weighing whether to add any caveat beyond that.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer, since the instruction is to reply with only yes or no and the Yes side does look more likely to win. I'm checking for any sign that the election has already happened, but the latest results pages I've seen show nothing certified, and the newest source is from November 2.

I'm going to run a couple more searches for any post-election Prop 3 results, then check the AIMSA poll details and the PPIC October report for the party breakdown and the ballot-label reading.

The historical data is useful. Support for measures usually sags before Election Day, but the decline is much smaller when the yes side has far more money than the opposition. I'll confirm there are no results yet, and check the AIMSA poll's methodology.

content.thinking:
I'm pulling the main figures from the CalMatters 2019 analysis: support drops about 6.6 to 7 points a month on average. The Kousser/NBER finding is that when the opposition more than doubles spending, support falls about twice as fast, while a well-funded backer keeps measures just above winning.

Now I'm checking the timing pattern: the sharpest declines show up in off-year and midterm primary contests, and much smaller ones before presidential general elections. A 2026 midterm general election is off-year, so the steeper drop-off could still apply. Voters also seem to sour faster on education and tax-raising measures than on bond or tax-cut measures, which matters for Prop 3.

Prop 3's net support barely moved from early September to late October, roughly a single point of erosion across seven weeks, well below the average monthly decline. That fits the pattern where a yes side with far more money holds its ground. The non-presidential timing still points toward some risk, so I'm weighing whether the funding edge outweighs it.

I'm estimating Prop 3's final margin: the current polls sit around +16 to +17 net, and I'm allowing a few points of erosion over the last ten days, which lands the expected final net somewhere near +12 to +16. I also want the sampling error, which for a poll of roughly 1,100 to 1,500 likely voters comes to about 2.7 points before adjusting for design effect.

I'm working out a probability for Prop 3 from the poll numbers and their error margins, which lands near 90% for a Yes win. I'm also checking the historical base rate, since tax measures have passed only about a third of the time, but extensions of existing taxes have done better than new ones.

I'm checking whether the 2012 and 2016 tax measures polled similarly before they passed, since that would give useful precedents for how this one might land. I'm also looking at how much of the early vote so far comes from older and white voters, because those groups tend to make up most of the early returns.

I'm checking whether older voters, who lean less toward Prop 3, are making up a bigger share of the early vote than the likely-voter model assumes. The October PPIC numbers show Central Valley support at 51%, and I want to see what the 55-and-older group looks like in that same report.

I'm working out whether older voters could drag the overall numbers below a majority. If they're about half the electorate at around 46% yes and younger voters are strongly in favor, the overall figure still lands above 50%. I'm now testing a scenario where older voters make up a larger share of the electorate to see where the margin breaks.

I'm checking whether older voters, who lean less toward Prop 3, could pull the overall number down, and running the math: even with them at 60% of the electorate, the yes side still lands around 55%. The softer spot is turnout among younger voters, since they tend to show up less in midterms, though the likely-voter model partly accounts for that.

I'm checking the September Berkeley IGS number for Prop 3 to see whether support has actually dropped since then. I'll also look for any late "No on 3" campaign, since the reported opposition spending so far is very small.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm pulling the Berkeley IGS figures from September and October: the September poll had 54% yes and 34% no, and October had 54% yes and 37% no. That puts the net margin down about three points over roughly five weeks.

Now I'm checking the other pollsters' numbers: PPIC went from 58-40 in September to 58-41 in October, a one-point dip in net support, and AIMSA has it at 56% yes. Taken together, support has held steady at a net of roughly +17 to +20 across pollsters and time. Campaign money is lopsided too, with the Yes side far ahead of the No side.

I'm weighing the 2016 precedent for a tax measure, where the October polls came in near the final result, and I'm noting that opposition was minimal then. I'm also considering a 2012 comparison, though it's not essential, since two precedents may be enough.

Now I'm comparing age groups: in 2016, 55+ voters backed the Prop 55 extension 50-37, while 2026 PPIC shows 55+ support for Prop 3 at 46%, so older voters have shifted somewhat against it even as overall support holds. Looking back at 2016, PPIC's support rose from 54% in September to 59% in October and ended at 63%, which suggests the late weeks can add support for an education-tax measure, and this year's polls have been steady. Taking that together, I'd put the Yes side's chances of winning at roughly 90 to 95 percent.

I'm weighing the risk of erosion over the last week or two before the vote, which might cost a few points of net support. The bigger question is whether polling could miss badly enough to flip a seventeen-point lead, and I'm considering measure polls that have been off by that much before.

I'm trying to recall how Prop 27 did in 2022, the online sports betting measure, where early polls had it well ahead but it ended up losing badly. That's a useful reminder that a large early lead doesn't guarantee a result.

I'm noting that the opposition in the 2022 sports betting case, mostly tribal money, drowned out early support, but here the No side has essentially no money, so that risk looks small. I'm also considering whether confusion with a similar measure could cut into the Yes side, though the Yes campaign has enough funds to answer that.

I'm checking the undecided share: even if every undecided voter broke no, the Yes side would still come out ahead in both the IGS and PPIC numbers, so the margin would need a sizable late shift to flip.

I'm now settling the answer format: the Yes side is the likelier winner, so the reply should be "yes," but I want to rule out reading the question as asking about the No side.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer, since the Yes side is the likelier winner, and I'm checking for any late polls or opposition spending that could shift that picture before I finalize.

I'm checking the campaign money totals, which vary by source, and I'm confirming that a measure passing is what counts as a win here. I'm also looking at whether any reporting on a possible legal challenge or the early-voter electorate could change that picture.

I'm double-checking the Berkeley IGS trend: its September and October polls both show 54% yes, with no yes-side movement, while the no share rose from 34 to 37 and undecideds fell from 13 to 8. PPIC is similarly steady at 58% yes both months.

I'm estimating the Yes side's chances at around 92-95%, given the steady 54-58% support and almost no organized opposition, and I'm weighing whether a last-minute spending push or a late poll shift could realistically reverse a 17-point lead.

I'm recalling a few earlier Prop 5 and Prop 15 results to test whether polling above 50 is enough, and what seems to decide these measures is money and a clear margin over 50.

I'm checking the wording of Prop 3 as a constitutional initiative, which needs only a simple majority under the state constitution, so there's no supermajority hurdle to clear.

I'm settling on the "yes" answer, since the question's framing points to the Yes side on Prop 3, and I'm treating that reading as settled.

I'm making a last check for any late-breaking news on Prop 3 from the final days, like a new opposition campaign or a poll showing it underwater. So far the sources I've seen show nothing negative, and the LA Times guide describes it as broadly supported.

I'm going to run one more search for late-breaking Prop 3 news from the last couple of days before the vote, to make sure nothing has shifted.
The historical precedent is strong: Prop 55 in 2016 polled 59% in October and won 63%. I'll run one last check for late-breaking news on Prop 3 from the final days of the campaign.

content.thinking:
I'm pulling up the details of a Berkeley IGS poll from late October: 54% of likely voters say they'll vote yes on Proposition 3, against 37% no. I want to check that figure against the SFGate article, which reports it as a finding that the measure is likely to pass.

Now I'm checking the other polling and the opposition funding: a PPIC survey from mid-October shows 58% yes and 41% no, and the September PPIC poll had 58% yes. On the money side, opponents have raised only about $5,500 while supporters have raised tens of millions, so I want to confirm the FPPC figures.

I'm worried the Yes on 3 campaign could get mixed up with the Prop 40 billionaire-tax ads, so voters might conflate the two. On the question itself, the polls point to the Yes side being more likely to win, which would make the answer "yes" if the question is whether the Yes side wins. I'm also weighing whether the question might instead be asking about the No side, since the wording is ambiguous.

I'm settling on the reading that the question asks whether the Yes side is more likely to win, so a "yes" answer would mean Yes wins. I still want to double-check whether the measure could fail, starting with the PPIC polls, which put Yes at 58% in both September and October.

Now I'm checking the Berkeley poll's 9% undecided and looking for other recent polls on Prop 3. I also want to read the Capital & Main piece, since the CFT's own numbers apparently came in lower than the September survey.

I'm going to check the Berkeley poll's details through its own publication and look for any other polls, since a closer race would change the picture. I also want to see whether any late-October news points to tightening on Prop 3 or a sudden opposition push.

I'm wondering whether the election has already happened, so I'll look for Prop 3 results first. I'm also planning a few parallel searches: the Berkeley IGS poll details, the Capital & Main piece on the campaign, and any opposition spending from the California Taxpayers Association.

California’s Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) , an ongoing tax on top income earners to help fund the state’s massive public education system, faces virtually no organized opposition. A September survey found that it enjoyed 58% support (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) among likely voters. It doesn’t create a new levy, either; it simply takes a tax that has been on the books since 2012 and makes it permanent.
So why are the measure’s supporters so nervous?
For the answer, look no further than a sample ballot for California’s Nov. 3 election. It’s bulging with 14 statewide propositions (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures), five of them involving tax questions of some kind.
That list includes Prop. 40, the so-called Billionaire Tax (https://capitalandmain.com/billionaires-shouldnt-exist-why-california-unions-are-fighting-for-a-wealth-tax), by far the largest and most controversial of the lot, along with two propositions that are expressly written to derail Prop. 40 if it is approved. And all of those measures were leading in the September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California, even though two of them are diametrically opposed to the third.
That’s a pretty solid sign that voters are baffled by the array of choices facing them. And for the teachers’ unions who say Prop. 3’s tax money is essential to the state’s education funding and some of their own members’ jobs, that is a worrisome place to be.
“While there’s no actual campaign against Prop. 3, I think a lot of people are confusing the ads against Prop. 40 and carrying that over to Prop. 3,” said Jeff Freitas, president of the California Federation of Teachers, which represents 120,000 education workers in the state. Freitas added that the CFT’s own polling numbers have come in lower than the robust showing in the September survey.
For those and other reasons, the CFT and the 310,000 strong California Teachers Association are rallying their members and using their money to help get out the vote in favor of Prop 3. (Disclosure: Both unions are financial supporters of Capital & Main.)
Their concern is understandable. At stake is $10 billion or more (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/) in education funding and essential services each year, a significant chunk of the state’s annual allocation for public schools from pre-K through community college.
“It’s a priority situation that we’re dealing with,” Freitas said.
* * *
California voters first passed a tax on high earners to safeguard education funding in 2012, when the state was facing heavy revenue losses following the Great Recession. Four years later, voters chose to extend the tax through 2030. Prop. 3 would remove the expiration date altogether.
The tax itself is straightforward: a slightly higher rate on the state’s top 2% (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016) of earners. In fiscal year 2025, that meant it applied only to individuals earning more than about $371,000, or $743,000 for married couples filing jointly, according to research (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/) by the California Budget & Policy Center.
Prop. 3 is also a tax on income only, not overall wealth. That’s an important distinction from the proposed Billionaire Tax, whose aim is to generate $100 billion in revenue over five years (primarily for health care funding) by placing a 5% one-time levy on the total net worth of the state’s roughly 250 billionaires.

But while proponents of the Billionaire Tax are only estimating what the state might receive from that measure, those pushing Prop. 3 have a clear idea about what the education tax revenues are worth. While the amount collected will vary, Freitas said the tax has been reliably worth $8 billion to $12 billion in annual public education funding in recent years.
That is upward of 10% of the state’s annual education budget. It has been a major boost. But that’s also what makes the prospect of Prop. 3 failing so concerning to the unions who represent hundreds of thousands of school teachers and support staff — and it’s the reason they’re not willing to take any chances.
* * *
The California Teachers Association has spent more than $33 million (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043) to qualify Prop. 3 for the ballot and rally support for it, and the California Federation of Teachers has added nearly $2 million more. Both unions are mobilizing their members to walk precincts and work phone banks as the vote draws closer.
In September, the CTA organized more than 1,000 of its members up and down the state to canvass neighborhoods and knock on doors. The goal was not only to talk up Prop. 3’s benefits, but to help voters distinguish it from the other tax measures on the November ballot.
The CTA includes on its website a tool that estimates how much funding (https://www.cta.org/our-advocacy/school-funding/yeson3) would be lost in each of California’s school districts if the tax extension fails. (Los Angeles Unified School District alone would be in line for a hit of more than $838 million per year.) The CTA estimates that one in six educators’ jobs would be at risk if the funding goes away.
There’s no ad campaign opposing Prop. 3. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which believes in strictly limiting government taxation, has weighed in against it (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/proposition-3-is-a-warning-against-proposition-40/), arguing that the education tax was created as a temporary measure in 2012 and touted again as temporary when it was renewed in 2016.
“The real lesson here is that whatever is represented to voters about a ballot measure seeking new programs or higher taxes should not be taken at face value,” Jon Coupal, president of the Jarvis association, wrote in a column (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/proposition-3-is-a-warning-against-proposition-40/) published on the organization’s website. Prop. 40, Coupal argued, should be viewed warily partly because of Prop. 3’s history.
It’s that conflation of tax measures — arguing against Prop. 40 and Prop. 3 at the same time, for example — that most concerns union leaders about the education tax’s chances of passage. And as the voters’ muddled response to the Public Policy Institute of California’s September survey demonstrated, there already appears to be plenty of mixed messaging out there.
“We’re getting school boards to pass resolutions [of support] for Prop. 3, we’re providing materials to our members, and we are definitely getting out there,” said CFT’s Freitas. It may take all that and more to ensure that the education tax doesn’t get lost in the shuffle come November.

A recent poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) from UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies released Thursday found Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm) is likely to pass, with 54% of likely voters saying they plan to vote yes, while 37% said they plan to vote no. It is the only measure out of seven that were surveyed that had more than 50% approval.

Prop. 3 is a tax measure that would make higher income tax rates permanent for single people who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $742,000. It would make permanent the existing tax rates, which are set to expire after 2030. If passed, 89% of tax revenue will continue to fund K-12 schools and the remaining 11% will go to community colleges.
These increased tax rates were initially passed by voters in 2012 during a budget deficit, and were extended by voters in 2016.
Each year, the high-income tax rates bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion for the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). The revenue has ranged year to year depending on earnings from the stock market and other outside factors. For those who earn over $1 million, that tax has been on top of another existing 1% tax that goes toward mental health services.

The ballot measure also has support from the National Education Association and the California School Employees Association. The opposition includes the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
While Prop. 3 appears to be gliding toward a win, polls are showing that Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire tax, is on track for failure. That measure would impose a new, one-time 5% tax on the financial assets of anyone who is worth $1 billion or more. If passed, 90% of the money would go toward funding healthcare to make up for an estimated $30 billion California (https://www.chcf.org/blog/2025/10/03/how-massive-federal-cuts-will-create-unprecedented-challenges-medi-cal-patients-providers/) will lose every year for Medicaid after Congress cut funding. Another 10 % would go to public education, food assistance and administration of the tax.
Prop. 40 has seen support drop in recent weeks (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/polling-proposition-40-22496894.php) as billionaire-funded opposition efforts ramped up. The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday that found the measure only has 46% of voters in favor of the billionaire tax. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that only 44% of voters are in support.

With contributors like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and billionaire investor John Doerr, the group has raised over $333 million, mostly going toward opposing Prop. 40 and supporting propositions 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php), making it one of the highest-funded ballot initiative efforts (https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/10/26/with-798-9-million-in-contributions-and-counting-2026-is-the-most-expensive-ballot-measure-election-cycle-in-california/) in California history.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

I'm recalling past extensions like Props 52, 55, and 56, which passed comfortably, and the failures like Prop 15 and the 2018 gas tax repeal, to see whether the comparison holds.

The PPIC numbers cut against that, though: Prop 3 sits at 58% yes while Prop 40 is only at 46%, so Prop 3 is clearly holding up better. Opposition spending is tiny compared with support, so the main risks I see are late erosion and turnout shifts.

I'm checking the historical record for California propositions with similar poll support, looking at how final polls compared with results, starting with Prop 30 in 2012.

I'm pulling together the historical comparisons now, recalling how final polls for Prop 30 in 2012 and Props 55 and 52 in 2016 lined up with their results. Since I'm not sure of the exact figures for those earlier polls, I'd like to check them before relying on them.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the electcademocrats.com tracker may lean partisan, so I'd rely on primary sources where I can. The IGS page lists Proposition 3's certified results as still pending. I'm also keeping in mind the CalMatters 2019 finding that public net support for ballot initiatives dropped by about 7 points a month on average.

I'm weighing the CalMatters finding that voter support for measures tends to erode closer to election day, with the steepest drops in midterm years like 2026. Prop 3's polls look flat from September to October, with net support around +17 to +18. I'm estimating that a typical monthly decline would shave maybe 3 points off that by election day, which still leaves a comfortable margin, though polling error could move it.

The math suggests Yes stays ahead even with some erosion, around 85-95% by my rough estimate. Tax measures tend to sour faster, which argues against Prop 3, though it's an extension and those usually poll better.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters article for more detail on how tax measures have held up, then check the PPIC blogs and the full October report for Prop 3's specific numbers and trend.

I'm checking the PPIC likely-voter trends and the October report for Prop 3's exact numbers, and I'm considering whether the midterm electorate's partisan mix shifts the support picture.

I'm checking whether any campaign against Prop 3 is funded enough to matter. The CalTax "No" committee looks small, and the billionaire-backed group that's targeting Props 40 through 42 doesn't appear to be spending on Prop 3.

I'm weighing a few risks on the No side: voters confusing Prop 3 with Prop 40 and voting no on both, the tendency of uncertain voters to default to no, fatigue from the number of tax measures, and the possibility that the ballot label shifts opinion. The polls were taken with the official ballot title and label in front of respondents, so those numbers should already reflect that wording.

I'm going to look at the 2019 CalMatters piece again for what it says about tax measures and the decline figures, then check the PPIC "Five Fast Takes" post and the Prop 3 numbers in their time-trends PDF.

content.text: The CalMatters analysis of historical polling suggests support often erodes before Election Day, especially for tax and education measures. I'll check the most recent PPIC commentary and the PPIC trend data for Prop 3.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. I'm pulling the main figures from the CalMatters 2019 analysis: support drops about 6.6 to 7 points a month on average. The Kousser/NBER finding is that when the opposition more than doubles spending, support falls about twice as fast, while a well-funded backer keeps measures just above winning.

Now I'm checking the timing pattern: the sharpest declines show up in off-year and midterm primary contests, and much smaller ones before presidential general elections. A 2026 midterm general election is off-year, so the steeper drop-off could still apply. Voters also seem to sour faster on education and tax-raising measures than on bond or tax-cut measures, which matters for Prop 3.

Prop 3's net support barely moved from early September to late October, roughly a single point of erosion across seven weeks, well below the average monthly decline. That fits the pattern where a yes side with far more money holds its ground. The non-presidential timing still points toward some risk, so I'm weighing whether the funding edge outweighs it.

I'm estimating Prop 3's final margin: the current polls sit around +16 to +17 net, and I'm allowing a few points of erosion over the last ten days, which lands the expected final net somewhere near +12 to +16. I also want the sampling error, which for a poll of roughly 1,100 to 1,500 likely voters comes to about 2.7 points before adjusting for design effect.

I'm working out a probability for Prop 3 from the poll numbers and their error margins, which lands near 90% for a Yes win. I'm also checking the historical base rate, since tax measures have passed only about a third of the time, but extensions of existing taxes have done better than new ones.

I'm weighing whether the Prop 3 case parallels earlier measures that passed with little funded opposition, like Prop 55 in 2016 and Prop 30 in 2012, which would suggest a passing margin around 60% or better. I'm also noting that the broader 2026 environment leans Democratic, which should favor a measure that Democrats back strongly, though some erosion from tax fatigue remains a possible risk.

I'm weighing the risks left for Prop 3: tax fatigue from the crowded ballot, and whether late opposition spending or a shift in how the measure is framed could peel off support. Late-counted ballots in California have leaned younger and more Democratic, which should help the yes side rather than hurt it. I'm checking the September Berkeley IGS number for Prop 3 to see whether support has actually dropped since then. I'll also look for any late "No on 3" campaign, since the reported opposition spending so far is very small.

Taken together, support has held steady at a net of roughly +17 to +20 across pollsters and time. Campaign money is lopsided too, with the Yes side far ahead of the No side.

I'm weighing the 2016 precedent for a tax measure, where the October polls came in near the final result, and I'm noting that opposition was minimal then. I'm also considering a 2012 comparison, though it's not essential, since two precedents may be enough.

Now I'm comparing age groups: in 2016, 55+ voters backed the Prop 55 extension 50-37, while 2026 PPIC shows 55+ support for Prop 3 at 46%, so older voters have shifted somewhat against it even as overall support holds. Looking back at 2016, PPIC's support rose from 54% in September to 59% in October and ended at 63%, which suggests the late weeks can add support for an education-tax measure, and this year's polls have been steady. Taking that together, I'd put the Yes side's chances of winning at roughly 90 to 95 percent.

I'm weighing the risk of erosion over the last week or two before the vote, which might cost a few points of net support. The bigger question is whether polling could miss badly enough to flip a seventeen-point lead, and I'm considering measure polls that have been off by that much before.

I'm trying to recall how Prop 27 did in 2022, the online sports betting measure, where early polls had it well ahead but it ended up losing badly. That's a useful reminder that a large early lead doesn't guarantee a result.

I'm noting that the opposition in the 2022 sports betting case, mostly tribal money, drowned out early support, but here the No side has essentially no money, so that risk looks small. I'm also considering whether confusion with a similar measure could cut into the Yes side, though the Yes campaign has enough funds to answer that.

I'm checking the undecided share: even if every undecided voter broke no, the Yes side would still come out ahead in both the IGS and PPIC numbers, so the margin would need a sizable late shift to flip.

I'm now settling the answer format: the Yes side is the likelier winner, so the reply should be "yes," but I want to rule out reading the question as asking about the No side.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer, since the Yes side is the likelier winner, and I'm checking for any late polls or opposition spending that could shift that picture before I finalize.

I'm checking the campaign money totals, which vary by source, and I'm confirming that a measure passing is what counts as a win here. I'm also looking at whether any reporting on a possible legal challenge or the early-voter electorate could change that picture.

I'm double-checking the Berkeley IGS trend: its September and October polls both show 54% yes, with no yes-side movement, while the no share rose from 34 to 37 and undecideds fell from 13 to 8. PPIC is similarly steady at 58% yes both months.

I'm estimating the Yes side's chances at around 92-95%, given the steady 54-58% support and almost no organized opposition, and I'm weighing whether a last-minute spending push or a late poll shift could realistically reverse a 17-point lead.

I'm recalling a few earlier Prop 5 and Prop 15 results to test whether polling above 50 is enough, and what seems to decide these measures is money and a clear margin over 50.

I'm checking the wording of Prop 3 as a constitutional initiative, which needs only a simple majority under the state constitution, so there's no supermajority hurdle to clear.

I'm settling on the "yes" answer, since the question's framing points to the Yes side on Prop 3, and I'm treating that reading as settled.

I'm making a last check for any late-breaking news on Prop 3 from the final days, like a new opposition campaign or a poll showing it underwater. So far the sources I've seen show nothing negative, and the LA Times guide describes it as broadly supported.
